question: Looking at AMD, what is the company's growth? What factors are responsible? Are those sustainable factors or just spikes?
answer:

  - U.S. export limits on China led to about $800M of MI308 charges, and about $360M was later reversed. [Advanced Micro Devices FY2025 10-K, p.64]

question: Why did Apple's profit drop in 2024 even though sales went up?
answer:
Apple's fiscal 2024 net income fell about 3%, to $93.7B from $97.0B, even though sales rose 2%. The cause was a one-time $10.2B tax charge. Apple's operating profit actually rose.

## What the filing says
- **Sales rose.** Net sales were $391.0B in 2024, up from $383.3B in 2023 (+2%) [Apple FY2024 10-K, p.25]. Services (subscriptions, App Store, advertising, cloud) grew 13% to $96.2B [Apple FY2024 10-K, p.26].
- **Operating profit rose.** Operating income (profit from the core business before taxes) was $123.2B, up from $114.3B [Apple FY2024 10-K, p.32]. Gross margin, which is sales minus the direct cost of making them, rose to $180.7B from $169.1B [Apple FY2024 10-K, p.32].
- **The tax bill jumped.** The provision for income taxes was $29.7B, up from $16.7B [Apple FY2024 10-K, p.32]. The effective tax rate, meaning the share of pre-tax profit paid as tax, went from 14.7% to 24.1% [Apple FY2024 10-K, p.28].
- **The reason was one-time.** Apple recorded a $10.2B net charge tied to the European Commission's "State Aid Decision," which ordered Ireland to recover extra taxes from Apple [Apple FY2024 10-K, p.28; p.42].
- **Net income fell.** Pre-tax income was $123.5B, and after taxes net income was $93.7B, down from $97.0B [Apple FY2024 10-K, p.32].
- **The charge did not repeat.** In 2025 the tax provision fell, partly because of a $10.7B year-over-year decrease in State Aid-related taxes [Apple FY2025 10-K, p.28].

## What this might mean
Apple's business made more money in 2024. The profit dip came from a one-off legal and tax matter, not weaker products. Without that $10.2B charge, net income would likely have risen. That is my arithmetic, not a figure the filing states.

question: What's the deal between Microsoft and OpenAI?
answer:
Microsoft's FY2026 10-K (year ended June 30, 2026) describes OpenAI as a long-term strategic partner and a major investment. Microsoft owns about 25% of OpenAI, it books large revenue from OpenAI, and it holds rights to OpenAI's technology.

## What the filing says
- **Partnership:** It began in 2019. Microsoft extended it in October 2025 and again in April 2026. Microsoft is "a major investor" and "will continue to receive revenue-sharing payments." [Microsoft FY2026 10-K, p.34]
- **Ownership:** Microsoft has an equity-method investment (it records its share of the investee's results) of roughly 25% on an as-converted basis. [Microsoft FY2026 10-K, p.60]
- **Money in:** Microsoft has committed $13.0 billion in total, and $11.9 billion had been funded by June 30, 2026. [Microsoft FY2026 10-K, p.60]
- **Money back:** Microsoft recorded $24.1 billion of FY2026 revenue from its commercial arrangements with OpenAI, including revenue-sharing. OpenAI owed Microsoft $6.0 billion in receivables at year-end. [Microsoft FY2026 10-K, p.60]
- **Technology rights:** Microsoft holds rights to OpenAI's intellectual property, including models and infrastructure, for use in its products. [Microsoft FY2026 10-K, p.34] The prior-year filing also said the OpenAI API was exclusive to Azure and that Microsoft had a right of first refusal on OpenAI's new capacity needs. [Microsoft FY2025 10-K, p.35] I didn't see those two terms repeated in the FY2026 passages I reviewed, so they may have changed.
- **Restructuring:** OpenAI formed a public benefit corporation and recapitalized in October 2025. Microsoft's ownership percentage fell as a result, and it recorded dilution gains. [Microsoft FY2026 10-K, p.60]
- **Earnings effect:** OpenAI investments raised FY2026 net income by $5.0 billion. In FY2025 they lowered it by $3.6 billion. [Microsoft FY2026 10-K, p.38]

## What this might mean
This is both an investment and a customer relationship. OpenAI spends heavily with Microsoft, which helps Azure, and Microsoft owns a share of OpenAI's outcome. Its profits can swing from year to year because of how OpenAI's results and ownership changes are accounted for. That is my reading, not the company's.

Tesla says it is "highly dependent" on Elon Musk, its CEO. This comes from the Tesla FY2025 10-K (year ended Dec 31, 2025). The filing also says he doesn't work only for Tesla.

## What the filing says
- Tesla states: "we are highly dependent on the services of Elon Musk, Technoking of Tesla and our Chief Executive Officer." Losing key employees could disrupt operations or delay product development and ramp-up. [Tesla FY2025 10-K, p.21]
- No key employee has an employment agreement for a set term. [Tesla FY2025 10-K, p.21]
- Musk "does not devote his full time and attention to Tesla." He also holds management positions at SpaceX, xAI, Neuralink and The Boring Company, and is involved in other ventures. [Tesla FY2025 10-K, p.22] The FY2024 10-K also listed X Corp. and the Department of Government Efficiency. [Tesla FY2024 10-K, p.23]
- In September 2025 the board granted Musk about 423.7 million performance-based restricted shares. Shareholders approved the grant on Nov 6, 2025. The award has 12 tranches, and each needs a market-value milestone and an operational milestone. [Tesla FY2025 10-K, p.84]
- Tesla says the award's product goals were designed to motivate Musk to spend time and energy on those products. It also warns that the goals may not match customer demand. [Tesla FY2025 10-K, p.29]
- Banks have lent to Musk against pledges of his Tesla stock. If he pledged shares and the price fell sharply, forced sales could push the stock down. [Tesla FY2025 10-K, p.29]

## What this might mean
This is my reading, not Tesla's. The company treats Musk as central to its success, and it has no contractual commitment to keep him. The large pay award looks like Tesla's way to keep his attention, though he has other companies that compete for his time. Tesla's fortunes are also tied to his personal finances, through the pledged-share risk.

question: How does a bank like JPMorgan make money?
answer:
JPMorgan Chase made money in 2025 in two main ways. It earned the gap between what it charges on loans and investments and what it pays on deposits. It also earned fees and trading revenue from services such as investment banking, payments, asset management and cards. Total net revenue was $182.4 billion, and net income was $57.0 billion.

## What the filing says
- **Two revenue streams.** Net interest income (NII) is interest earned minus interest paid. It was $95.4 billion, about 52% of revenue. Noninterest revenue is fees, trading and similar income. It was $87.0 billion, about 48%. [JPMorgan Chase FY2025 10-K, p.49]
- **Interest-earning assets.** Loans averaged $1.4 trillion and earned a 6.72% rate. Total interest-earning assets averaged $3.83 trillion and earned 5.05%. [JPMorgan Chase FY2025 10-K, p.317]
- **Three business segments, 2025 managed-basis revenue.** Managed basis is the company's adjusted view for segment reporting. [JPMorgan Chase FY2025 10-K, p.66]
  - Consumer & Community Banking: $76.0 billion.
  - Commercial & Investment Bank: $78.5 billion.
  - Asset & Wealth Management: $24.1 billion.
  - Corporate: $7.0 billion.
- **Consumer bank.** It makes money from card and loan interest, deposits, and fees such as asset management, deposit and auto lease income. [JPMorgan Chase FY2025 10-K, p.68]
- **Commercial & Investment Bank.** Markets revenue (trading) was $35.8 billion, Payments was $19.3 billion, and Investment Banking was $10.2 billion. [JPMorgan Chase FY2025 10-K, pp.73]
- **Costs and risk.** Noninterest expense was $95.6 billion. The firm also set aside $14.2 billion for expected loan losses (provision for credit losses). [JPMorgan Chase FY2025 10-K, p.49]

## What this might mean
This is my reading, not the company's. JPMorgan is a mix of a lender, a payments and trading business, and a fee-earning wealth manager. That mix means no single source decides its results. Interest income is sensitive to rates, and trading and deal fees depend on market activity.

question: How much money do customers keep at JPMorgan?
answer:
Customers kept about $2.56 trillion in deposits at JPMorgan Chase at December 31, 2025 (FY2025 10-K). That's up from $2.41 trillion a year earlier. I'm reading "money customers keep" as deposits, meaning money held in accounts at the bank.

- **Consumer segment trend:** Consumer & Community Banking's average deposits fell 1% in 2025. The commercial and investment bank's average client deposits rose 14%. [JPMorgan Chase FY2025 10-K, p.51]

question: How much did JPMorgan set aside for bad loans?
answer:
JPMorgan Chase set aside $14.2 billion for credit losses (its "provision for credit losses") in 2025, the year ended December 31, 2025. That's up from $10.7 billion in 2024. A provision is money a bank expenses now to cover loans that may not be repaid.

## What the filing says
- The 2025 provision was $14,212 million, compared with $10,678 million in 2024 and $9,320 million in 2023. [JPMorgan Chase FY2025 10-K, p.55]
- The provision has two parts. Net charge-offs were $9.8 billion. These are loans written off as uncollectible, minus amounts later recovered. The other part was a $4.4 billion net addition to the allowance, which is the cushion held for future losses. [JPMorgan Chase FY2025 10-K, p.55]
- Consumer lending made up $11.5 billion of the provision. Credit cards accounted for $10.8 billion of that, and card net charge-offs were driven by loan growth. [JPMorgan Chase FY2025 10-K, p.55]
- Wholesale lending (loans to companies and institutions) made up $2.7 billion. This included estimated losses from borrower fraud in certain secured lending facilities. [JPMorgan Chase FY2025 10-K, p.55]
- $2.2 billion of the consumer allowance increase related to the Apple Card transaction. [JPMorgan Chase FY2025 10-K, p.55]
- The total allowance for credit losses stood at $31.2 billion at year-end 2025. [JPMorgan Chase FY2025 10-K, p.131]

## What this might mean
The bigger provision came from two things: more actual card losses as lending grew, and a larger cushion built up. Some of that cushion was tied to the Apple Card deal and to caution about the economic outlook. That is my reading, not the company's. The filing doesn't say the loans are going bad faster than expected.

question: Is NVIDIA investing in AI companies that in turn are buying their chips/services? Is this also true for AMD?
answer:
**Yes for NVIDIA, and partly for AMD.** In fiscal 2026 (year ended Jan 25, 2026), NVIDIA said some of its startup investments go to AI model makers that buy its products. AMD's version works differently. In 2025 it gave OpenAI the right to buy AMD shares, tied to OpenAI buying AMD chips.

## What the filing says
- NVIDIA invested $17.5 billion in private companies and infrastructure funds in fiscal 2026, mainly early-stage startups. The filing says these "include AI model makers that purchase our products directly or through CSPs" (cloud service providers). [NVIDIA FY2026 10-K, p.37]
- NVIDIA also gave $3.5 billion in land, power and shell guarantees to early-stage companies, generally over multiple years. If those companies can't pay, NVIDIA may take over the leases. [NVIDIA FY2026 10-K, p.37]
- NVIDIA warns that many of these investments are illiquid, the startups may never be profitable, and there is no assurance it will earn a return. [NVIDIA FY2026 10-K, p.37]
- AMD signed a deal in October 2025 with OpenAI to deploy 6 gigawatts of AMD GPUs, starting with 1 gigawatt of MI450 chips. [AMD FY2025 10-K, p.64]
- Alongside that deal, AMD issued OpenAI a warrant (a right to buy shares) for up to 160 million AMD shares at $0.01 each. The shares vest in tranches as OpenAI hits GPU purchase milestones and AMD stock price targets. None had vested as of Dec 27, 2025, so there was no financial impact that year. [AMD FY2025 10-K, p.103]

## What this might mean
This is my reading, not the companies'. NVIDIA is putting cash into customers, which can help fund their chip purchases. AMD is offering equity as an incentive for a customer to buy. Both links tie a supplier's results to its customers' health. The passages I found don't say how much of each company's revenue comes from these specific investees.
